# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

messages.content:
# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits

function.name: push

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.

- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.

function.name: push

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.

You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. # Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.

- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.

- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.

- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done

function.name: unload

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits

function.name: push

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat

function.name: tighten_to

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

We have a UR16e arm on a Husky base. The socket is fixed to wrist 3. We need to tighten an M8 bolt to 14-18 N·m (aim ~16 N·m).

Bolt head top center: (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m. Bolt axis: (0, 0.342, 0.940) — pointing out of the head. So the bolt axis points in +y and +z direction (mostly z up, slightly y left). Wait, the axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). So the head top is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439), and the axis goes outward in direction (0, 0.342, 0.940). So the bolt extends from the head in that direction. The socket needs to approach along the axis (tool z pointing along the axis, pointing out of the socket). Hmm, tool z points out of the socket, along socket axis. For the socket to go onto the bolt head, the socket axis must align with bolt axis, and socket z points along bolt axis direction (out of the head). Actually the socket is placed over the bolt head: the socket face opens toward the head, socket z points out of socket, i.e., away from the head along the bolt axis direction.

Wait, tool z points out of the socket. So to seat onto the bolt head, the socket z should point along the bolt axis (out of head direction) and the socket face (opening) faces the head. So socket position is along the axis beyond the head top, i.e., at head_top + depth * axis_direction. The socket face is 0.16 m from wrist flange on wrist-3 axis (tool z). So socket face position = tool position + 0.16 * tool_z (approximately, ignoring tool frame origin offset... actually tool frame origin is at centre of socket's open face). So tool position = socket face center position.

The ready aims provided:
- Centre on axis where it is now: aim [0.42000, 0.05820, 0.55773], socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]
- Centre 0.5 mm out from head top: aim [0.42000, 0.01517, 0.43947], socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]
- 50 mm out: aim [0.42000, 0.03210, 0.48599], socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]

Wait, socket_toward is [0, -0.3419, -0.9397] which is negative of bolt axis (0, 0.342, 0.940). Hmm. So socket z points opposite to bolt axis? Let me think.

Bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). The socket z points out of the socket. If the socket is on the head, socket face opens toward the head, socket z points away from head, i.e., along bolt axis direction (out of head). So socket z should be (0, 0.342, 0.940). But the ready aim says socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397], which is opposite. Hmm, that's the direction the tool z points... Let me reconsider.

Maybe the aim point is where the socket face center should be. For the "50 mm out" aim: aim [0.420, 0.03210, 0.48599], socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]. Difference from head top: (0, 0.0171, 0.04699). Length: sqrt(0.0171² + 0.04699²) = sqrt(0.000292 + 0.002208) = sqrt(0.0025) = 0.05 m = 50 mm. Direction: (0, 0.342, 0.940). So the aim point is 50 mm along the bolt axis from the head top. But socket_toward is [0, -0.3419, -0.9397], opposite direction. That means tool z points back toward the head? That seems wrong...

Wait, maybe I misread. Let's recompute: aim point for 50 mm out = head_top + 50mm * axis_dir = (0.420, 0.015 + 0.05*0.342, 0.439 + 0.05*0.940) = (0.420, 0.0321, 0.486). Yes matches. So the aim point is 50 mm out along the bolt axis. But socket_toward is negative of axis. Hmm, that would mean the socket points back at the head, i.e., socket face points away from the head. That can't seat.

Hold on — maybe the convention: socket z points out of the socket, and to put the socket onto the bolt, you approach the head with socket z pointing toward the head? No: socket is a cylinder open at one end (the face). Tool frame origin at centre of socket's open face, z along socket's axis pointing out of the socket. So z points out of the open face, away from the socket's interior. If the socket is on the bolt head, the open face is toward the bolt head (socket surrounds the head), and z points out of the socket, i.e., away from the head, along the bolt axis direction (out of head). So socket z = bolt axis direction = (0, 0.342, 0.940).

But the ready aim uses [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]. Hmm, that's confusing. Unless the bolt axis given points out of the head but the socket approaches from the other side? Let's check the current socket state: socket points along tool z = (0.1070, 0.0055, -0.9942), mostly -z (down). Head top at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439). Socket at (0.2465, 0.1772, 0.5144). The socket is 126 mm short of head top, axis off by 214 mm, tilted 21 deg.

The ready aim socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397] points mostly down (-z) and -y. The aim points are above the head (z=0.486 for 50mm out, head z=0.439). So tool z points from aim point down toward... aim point + socket_toward*something: from (0.420, 0.0321, 0.486) going along (0, -0.3419, -0.9397) goes to lower y and lower z, toward the head top and beyond. So tool z points from the aim point toward the head and past it. That means the socket's open face... hmm.

Actually wait: maybe the approach is that the socket is placed over the bolt head from above, with socket z pointing toward the head (i.e., into the socket? No, z points out of socket). If socket z points toward the head, then the open face (at tool origin) faces away from the head — that doesn't make sense for seating.

Hmm, let me reconsider. Perhaps "z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket" means pointing out the back end? Actually for a socket wrench, the square drive is at the back, hex opening at front. Tool z along axis pointing out of the socket — out of which end? If the socket's open face is the hex opening (front), and z points out of the socket... ambiguous.

Given the ready aims are computed by the system and are presumably correct, let's just trust them: socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397] is the tool z direction when seated. Unless the bolt axis "points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940)" means the bolt shaft extends in that direction from the head, so to put a socket on the head you come from the opposite side? The socket sits on the head, surrounding it, and the socket's axis aligns with bolt axis. The head top is the top of the head; the bolt shaft goes out from the head in direction (0,0.342,0.940). So socket position = head_top - (depth) * shaft_direction, and socket z (pointing out of open face toward the head... hmm.

OK this is getting confusing. Let me just think practically: The aim points computed: head_top + 50mm * bolt_axis. Wait if z points from socket toward head, and z points "out of the socket", then the open face is the side facing the head, and z points out of it toward the head. The head top is at aim - 50mm*axis. The socket face at aim, opening toward the head (direction -axis). The socket depth is 0.16 m from flange... anyway.

So actually the geometry: bolt head top at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439). Socket face needs to be at head_top plus some amount along axis such that the head top is at least 2.5 mm inside the socket. The socket face plane is perpendicular to axis at socket position. The head top is "inside the socket" means the head top has entered past the socket face into the socket interior. The socket interior extends from the face in direction -z (into the socket). Since z = -axis, socket interior is in direction +axis from the face? No wait: z points out of the socket (toward the head, direction -axis from aim point). Interior is opposite z, i.e., +axis direction from the face. Hmm, that puts interior beyond the head top along the bolt shaft. The head top at aim - d*axis. For the head top to be inside the socket, the face must be beyond the head top in -axis direction? I'm confusing myself.

Let me just define: unit vector a = bolt axis = (0, 0.342, 0.940) (out of head). Socket face center position p. Socket z = -a (from the ready aims, socket_toward = -a normalized: (0, -0.3419, -0.9397) ≈ -a since a = (0,0.342,0.940), |a|=1). So socket z points toward the head (from p to head_top is roughly -a direction if p = head_top + 50mm*a).

Socket interior: socket is a tube; open face at p, extends in direction -z = +a from p. So socket covers points p + t*a for t in [0, depth]. Head top h = p - 50mm*a (for the 50mm-out pose). For head top to be inside socket: h = p + t*a for some t in [0, socket_depth]. But h = p - 0.05*a, so t = -0.05, not in [0, depth]. Contradiction. So the socket interior must be in direction -a from p, i.e., socket z = +a points out of the socket (interior behind face in -z = -a direction). But socket_toward says z = -a...

Hmm, maybe the socket extends in direction z from the face (z points out of socket means out of the back?). Let me reinterpret: "origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket." If z points out of the socket from the open face, then the socket body is on the -z side of the face. With z = -a, body is in +a direction from p. Head top h = p - 0.05a is on the -a side, i.e., outside the socket body — but that's where the head should enter... 

Alternatively maybe I have the bolt axis direction wrong: "its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940)". Hmm.

OK, maybe the ready aim's socket_toward being -a is intentional: the socket approaches the head with its open face toward the head, z pointing into the open face? function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

messages.content:
# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m
