# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

function.name: seat

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

Let me analyze the situation.

We have a UR16e arm on a parked Husky. We need to tighten an M8 bolt to 14-18 N·m (aim ~15.5-16), then retract the socket more than 30 mm from the head top.

The bolt head top center is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m, axis pointing out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). Wait, "axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940)". That means the bolt axis (direction from head into the part, i.e., out of the head) is y=0.342, z=0.940. So the bolt goes into the module in the direction +y, +z.

The socket z axis points out of the socket. To seat the socket onto the bolt, the socket z should point along the bolt axis (out of the head) — i.e., socket z pointing (0, 0.342, 0.940), so the socket approaches the head from... hmm. Let's think: The socket's open face is at the tool origin, z along the socket axis pointing out of the socket. The socket goes over the bolt head. The bolt head top is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439). The bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). So the socket should be positioned with its face near the head top, and socket z pointing along the bolt axis direction (out of the head). The socket face is 0.16 m from wrist-3 flange along wrist-3 axis.

The ready aims given:
- centre where it is now: aim [0.42000, 0.05346, 0.54470], toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]
- centre 0.5 mm out from head top: aim [0.42000, 0.01517, 0.43947], toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]
- 50 mm out: aim [0.42000, 0.03210, 0.48599], toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]

Interesting: socket_toward is [0, -0.3419, -0.9397], which is the negative of the bolt axis (0, 0.342, 0.940). Hmm. So socket z points opposite to the bolt axis direction "out of the head". Let's think about geometry.

The bolt axis "points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940)". So the head top is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439), and the bolt extends from the head in direction (0, 0.342, 0.940)? Actually "out of the head" — the head is on the outside, the bolt shank goes into the module. The axis pointing out of the head would point toward the viewer, away from the module. Hmm, but the socket needs to go over the head from the outside.

The socket face is at the tool origin; the socket extends 0.16 m from the flange along wrist-3 axis (tool z? "The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis." and tool z is along the socket's axis pointing out of the socket). So the socket extends from the flange in the +tool z direction? The socket's face (open face) is at the tool frame origin? "Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket." So the open face is at the tool origin, and the socket body extends in -z direction (into the socket), while z points out of the socket (toward the bolt head and beyond).

Wait, but then "The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis." The wrist-3 flange is at some offset from the tool origin along... the tool z axis presumably. If the socket face is at the tool origin, and the flange is 0.16 m from the face on the wrist-3 axis, then the flange is at -0.16 * z from the tool origin (z points out of the socket, away from the flange). So the flange is behind the socket face.

Now to seat the socket on the bolt head: the socket open face needs to be at the head top, with socket z pointing along the bolt axis so the socket goes over the head. The bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940) — this is the direction from the head toward... outside? If the axis points out of the head, then the socket z should point in the same direction (out of the socket = toward and beyond the head). Hmm, but the socket goes over the head: the open face is at the head, and the socket extends back from the head (away from the part) in the direction opposite to the bolt shank.

Actually let's reconsider: bolt head sits on the surface; the shank goes into the material. The axis "pointing out of the head" points away from the material, toward the robot. The socket approaches from outside, its open face over the head, socket axis aligned with bolt axis, socket z pointing out of the socket (further out beyond the head). So socket z should be parallel to the bolt axis direction (0, 0.342, 0.940). But the ready aim says socket_toward = [0, -0.3419, -0.9397], which is opposite. Hmm.

Wait, maybe the bolt axis as given points into the module (the shank direction), and "out of the head" means from the top of the head going into... hmm. Let's check the head top at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439). The current tool position is (0.2345, 0.1936, 0.4937). The vector from tool to head top: (0.1855, -0.1786, -0.0547). The current socket z (tool z) points (0.0225, 0.0450, -0.9987) — mostly downward. The socket is currently pointing down, not at the bolt.

The ready aim "to centre the socket on the axis where it is now": aim point [0.42000, 0.05346, 0.54470], toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]. So the socket face would be at (0.42, 0.053, 0.545), pointing with z along (0, -0.342, -0.940). That means the socket extends from its face in the -z direction = (0, 0.342, 0.940) — into the head/module. So the socket face is above/out from the head, and the socket body extends along (0, 0.342, 0.940) over the bolt head. Hmm, that means the socket's open face is at the head top and the socket extends further along the bolt axis beyond the head? That doesn't make physical sense for a socket over a bolt head.

Wait, maybe I have the direction backwards. "z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket." If the socket is over the bolt head, the open face is at the top (toward the robot), and the socket body extends down onto the head (away from the robot). So z pointing out of the socket points toward the robot (away from the head). The bolt axis "pointing out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940)" points from the head toward the robot/outside. So socket z should be parallel to the bolt axis: (0, 0.342, 0.940). But the ready aim uses (0, -0.3419, -0.9397) = negative of that. Hmm.

Hold on, maybe the bolt axis points into the part: the head top is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439), and the bolt goes into the module along (0, 0.342, 0.940). Then "out of the head" describes the axis line direction from the head into... ugh.

Let's just use the ready aims provided. The system computed them from the work order numbers. The aim point for "centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top" is [0.42000, 0.01517, 0.43947], which is essentially the head top (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) offset slightly along... the difference is (0, 0.00017, 0.00047) — about 0.5 mm along the bolt axis (0, 0.342, 0.940) normalized? (0, 0.342, 0.940) has norm ~1.002, so unit ~(0, 0.341, 0.938). 0.5 mm along that = (0, 0.00017, 0.00047). Yes! So the aim point is 0.5 mm from the head top along the bolt axis direction (0, 0.342, 0.940). And socket_toward = (0, -0.3419, -0.9397) is opposite to the bolt axis.

So the convention: socket face is placed at a point along the bolt axis beyond the head top (in the direction the axis points), and the socket z points back toward the head (opposite to the axis direction). That means the bolt axis "points out of the head" toward the socket/robot side. So the socket sits on the head with its face outside the head, z pointing from socket face toward the head and into the part. The socket extends from its face in -z = (0, 0.342, 0.940) direction, i.e., onto the head and into the part. That makes sense: socket face is the open end near the robot, socket body goes over the head toward the part.

OK so the approach: move to the "50 mm out" aim: socket face 50 mm from head top along bolt axis, i.e., at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) + 0.05*(0, 0.342, 0.940) = (0.420, 0.0321, 0.4860). Matches the given ready aim [0.42000, 0.03210, 0.48599]. Good.

Then the seat procedure: start with socket on axis just off head top, reached in two aims: first the 50 mm out aim, then the "centre it 0.5 mm out from head top" aim. Then call seat.

Then tighten_to with torque ~16 N·m.

Then unload, then retract to >30 mm (e.g., 50 mm).

Also need to check the bolt is "snug" — installed torque near zero until snug. tighten_to turns until drive torque reaches the setpoint; it slows near end. We just set torque_Nm = 16 (or 15.5). The accepted window is 14-18.

Wrist 3 limit: at most one full turn either way from zero. The bolt starts between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug. So we need to turn up to 212 degrees to reach snug, plus more to reach torque. Wrist 3 can turn at most one full turn (360 deg) from zero; current wrist3 position is -0.0226 rad (~-1.3 deg). We have plenty of range (about 358 deg available in one direction). The turn needed: up to ~212 deg to snug plus tightening angle to reach 16 N·m. For an M8 bolt, torque 16 N·m might require maybe 60-180 deg beyond snug depending on friction. Total could approach or exceed 360? Hmm. The instructions say if a job needs more rotation than is left, lift socket, turn back, seat again. But we have ~358 deg of wrist3 travel available. Snug requires at most 212 deg. Then to reach 16 N·m... Let's think: M8 clamp bolt, torque 16 N·m. Typical torque-angle: snug then maybe 30-90 deg to reach torque. So total maybe 212+90 = 302 deg < 360. Probably OK in one go. But tighten_to only turns until torque reached; it's a closed loop. The turn command is limited to 90 deg per call, but tighten_to handles it internally.

Actually, the turn limits: "turn about its own z axis... At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90." That's for the turn tool. tighten_to is a closed loop that turns as needed. It might internally handle multiple turns? It says "turn the seated socket in the tightening direction... stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm." It presumably can turn more than 90 deg since it's a closed loop with time limit. Let's assume it can.

But also there's the 30-second total time limit. seat (default 10 s), tighten_to (default 15 s) — that's already 25 s plus movement time. Hmm, we have only 30 s total. We need to be efficient.

Wait, "You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed." So total time across all commands is 30 seconds? That's tight. Each command takes time to execute. The arm moves at limited speeds. Let's estimate: current tool position (0.2345, 0.1936, 0.4937) to aim point (0.42, 0.0321, 0.486): distance ~ sqrt(0.1855² + 0.1615² + 0.0077²) ≈ sqrt(0.0344 + 0.0261) ≈ sqrt(0.0605) ≈ 0.246 m. Arm max speed: shoulder joints 2.094 rad/s; TCP speed could be maybe ~1 m/s. So move takes ~0.3-0.5 s. Fine.

Plan:
1. aim to 50 mm out: aim([0.420, 0.0321, 0.486], [0, -0.342, -0.940]). Actually we can use the exact given ready aim.
2. aim to 0.5 mm out: aim([0.420, 0.01517, 0.43947], [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]).
3. seat(max_s=10) — engages socket.
4. tighten_to(torque_Nm=16, max_s=15).
5. unload().
6. retract(mm=50).
7. done.

But time: aim commands move the arm; each aim is a motion that completes before returning ("the arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives... the tool's result then tells us"). So each aim takes some seconds. seat up to 10 s but should end when seated quickly. tighten_to up to 15 s but ends when torque reached. unload quick. retract quick.

Total 30 s is tight but probably OK if motions are fast. Let's consider using lower max_s for seat to save time? seat ends when seated; default 10 s. If seating takes 1-2 s, fine.

Actually, maybe we can combine: The aim tool description says "from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head." So aim handles the approach automatically — if we aim directly at the head-top point, it will first go to 50 mm out then close in. But the seat procedure explicitly requires two aims: first 50 mm out, then 0.5 mm out, then seat. Let's follow that.

Alternatively, one aim to the 0.5 mm out point might auto-stop at 50 mm first. But the instructions for seat say to reach it in two aims. Let's do two aims to be safe.

Concern: wrist 3 one-full-turn limit. Current wrist3 = -0.0226 rad. Zero is presumably where the socket flats align... hmm, "Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero." Zero is the home position of wrist 3. Current position -0.0226 rad ≈ -1.3°, so nearly at zero. We can turn up to ~358° in either direction before hitting the limit. The bolt needs up to 212° to snug, then tightening to 16 N·m. For an M8 bolt with nut factor K=0.2, T = K*d*F => F = 16/(0.2*0.008) = 10000 N clamp. The turn-to-torque angle depends on friction; typical might be 60-120° after snug. Total worst case 212 + 120 = 332° < 358°. Should be OK but cutting close. If it exceeds, tighten_to would hit the joint limit and stop without reaching torque. Hmm.

Actually, does the joint limit stop tighten_to? "A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached." For tighten_to, it turns until torque reached or time or socket comes off. If wrist 3 hits its limit, it can't turn further; presumably it stops. Risk of failure.

Alternative: We could first turn the bolt toward snug manually? We don't know how far short of snug it is (149-212°). We could just let tighten_to do its thing: it turns slowly, torque rises near snug and continues to 16. It will stop at 16 N·m or at joint limit.

Given the random start "between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug", and the judge checks "The bolt has been turned until it is snug" and "installed torque reached 14 N·m". If we stop at 16 N·m installed, both satisfied (assuming snug occurs before 14 N·m, which it does — torque near zero until snug).

Time estimate for tighten_to: turning at "turn slowly" — maybe 10-30 deg/s? If we need ~300° of rotation, at 30 deg/s that's 10 s; at 10 deg/s, 30 s — too long! Hmm. The max_s default is 15 s. If tightening takes longer than 15 s, it stops early and we fail (torque not reached). We can set max_s up to... we have 30 s total. Let's allocate: aim1 ~0.5 s, aim2 ~0.3 s, seat ~1 s, tighten_to up to 15 s, unload ~1 s, retract ~0.5 s. Total ~18 s. OK within 30 s.

But how fast does tighten_to turn? "turn slowly" — unknown. Let's just try with max_s=15 and torque 16. If it stops due to time without reaching torque, we may need another tighten_to call (wrist3 position continues from where it stopped; the limit is from zero, cumulative). Actually if tighten_to hits max_s without reaching torque, we can call tighten_to again (socket still seated, loaded). But each call has overhead.

Let's think about the angle needed more carefully. The bolt starts 149-212° short of snug. Suppose worst case 212° to snug. Then torque ramps from 0 to 16 N·m over some angle. For M8, pitch 1.25 mm. Torque 16 N·m → clamp force ~ 10 kN (K=0.2). Bolt elongation: F = k*ΔL, k = AE/L = (π/4 * 0.008² * 200e9)/L. For L=0.02 m: A=5e-5 m², AE=1e7 N, k=5e8 N/m. ΔL = 10000/5e8 = 20 μm. Thread advance per radian: pitch/(2π) = 1.25e-3/6.283 = 0.199 mm/rad = 199 μm/rad. So 20 μm elongation = 0.1 rad = 5.7° of bolt stretch plus embedding. So once snug, only ~10-20° more to reach 16 N·m! Most rotation is just taking up the gap to snug (149-212°). So total rotation ~160-230°. Well within 358°.

Time at "slowly": if turn speed is, say, 30 deg/s (0.5 rad/s), 230° takes ~7.7 s. Within 15 s. Probably fine.

But wait — there's a subtlety: installed torque near zero until snug. tighten_to stops when drive torque reaches torque_Nm. Drive torque includes friction in the thread; once snug, torque rises quickly. Good.

Also the socket must be seated properly: "top of head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket". The socket face is 0.16 m from flange; socket depth over head — seat handles engagement.

Hex alignment: socket only goes over head when flats line up (every 60°). seat handles unwinding if a corner catches.

Let's also consider: do we need to aim at all, or can we just call seat directly? seat requires starting "with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims". So we must do the two aims first.

Current tool pose: position (0.2345, 0.1936, 0.4937), z pointing (0.0225, 0.0450, -0.9987) — pointing down. The first aim moves to (0.42, 0.0321, 0.486) with z along (0, -0.342, -0.940). That's a big reorientation. Should be reachable.

Let me now also double check the direction sign for tightening: "A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread." Tool z points from socket face toward the head (into the part). Seen from behind the tool (looking from the part side toward the robot? "behind the tool" = looking along -z? or from the tool's perspective behind?). Positive rotation tightens. tighten_to turns in the tightening direction. Good, we just call tighten_to.

One more consideration: the force-torque sensor reads torque about tool z equal to tightening torque (negative while tightening). tighten_to uses "the wrist's drive torque". Fine.

Now the 30-second limit: We should be mindful. Let's start.

First command: aim to the 50 mm out point.

aim: {"aim": [0.42000, 0.03210, 0.48599], "socket_toward": [0.0000, -0.3419, -0.9397]}

Then aim to 0.5 mm out: {"aim": [0.42000, 0.01517, 0.43947], "socket_toward": [0.0000, -0.3419, -0.9397]}

Then seat. Then tighten_to(16). Then unload. Then retract(50). Then done.

Should we worry that aim might not reach exactly due to joint limits? The arm will get as close as possible. The readings will tell us.

Also note: The socket face is 0.16 m from the flange. The aim point is where the socket's open face (tool origin) goes. Good, the aim tool puts "the centre of the socket's open face at a point". 

Let's begin with the first aim.

Actually, wait — should I include both aims in one turn? "call exactly one tool each turn." So one tool per response. I'll do aim #1 now.

Let me also think about whether we can skip aiming and just go: The current socket is far off axis (237 mm off). We must aim first anyway.

1. aim to 50mm out point.
2. aim to 0.5mm out point.
3. seat() — engages.
4. tighten_to(torque_Nm=16.0, max_s=15).
5. unload().

Total ~15 s. Within 30 s.

Also, should tighten_to max_s be 15 (default)? Yes.

Potential issue: If the bolt requires more rotation than wrist3 has left (~358° from -1.3°), tighten_to might stall at the joint limit. Worst case 212° to snug + ~20° to torque = 232°. Fine.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.

- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.

function.name: turn

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.

## Limits

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.

- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. function.name: unload

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.
