# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.

- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.

- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. ## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.

- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

messages.reasoning_content:
Let me analyze the situation.

We have a UR16e arm on a Husky base (parked). Tool: 13mm hex socket fixed to wrist 3. Socket face is 0.16m from wrist-3 flange along tool z axis.

Work order: tighten M8 clamp bolt. Bolt head top center at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m. Axis points out of head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940) — so mostly up (z) and slightly left (y). Wait, axis points "out of the head" — the bolt's axis direction. So the bolt goes into the module along -axis direction? Actually the axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). So the bolt shaft goes into the head in the opposite direction: (0, -0.342, -0.940).

The socket's z axis points out of the socket. To seat the socket on the bolt, the socket's z axis should align with the bolt's axis (pointing out of the head). Wait — the socket goes onto the head from outside. The bolt axis points out of the head (toward where the socket would approach). So socket z should point along the bolt axis direction: (0, 0.342, 0.940).

Current socket points along (0.1111, 0.0286, -0.9934) — pointing mostly down. That's quite different. So we need to reorient significantly.

Given readings:
- Socket face is 126.74 mm short of head top (distance along... well, just distance).
- Socket axis off bolt axis: 215.68 mm (centre at -169.50, 125.34, -45.60 mm from axis).
- Tilted 22.52 deg.

Ready aims provided:
1. Centre where it is now: aim [0.42000, 0.05833, 0.55810], toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]
2. Centre 0.5 mm out from head top: aim [0.42000, 0.01517, 0.43947], toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]
3. 50 mm out: aim [0.42000, 0.03210, 0.48599], toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]

Wait, the socket_toward is [0, -0.3419, -0.9397], which is the NEGATIVE of the bolt axis. Hmm. The bolt axis points out of head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). The socket_toward given is [0, -0.3419, -0.9397], which points INTO the head (opposite). That seems odd. Let me think.

Actually, the socket's z axis points OUT of the socket (toward where the fastener would go). To put the socket onto the bolt head, the socket approaches the head with its open face toward the head. The socket z points out of the socket open face. So when the socket is on the bolt, socket z points away from the head, i.e., along the bolt axis (out of head). So socket_toward should be (0, 0.342, 0.940).

But the provided ready aims use [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]. Hmm, maybe they define "socket_toward" as the direction the socket points to approach the head? Actually for "aim" tool: "Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction". The open face points along socket z. So socket_toward should be the direction from the socket face outward.

Wait, but if we're 50 mm out on the axis, the socket face is at head_top + 50mm * (axis direction)? If axis points out of head, then 50 mm out on the axis means position = head_top + 0.05 * axis = (0.420, 0.015 + 0.0171, 0.439 + 0.047) = (0.420, 0.0321, 0.486). That matches the 50mm aim: [0.42000, 0.03210, 0.48599]. Good. And socket_toward there is [0, -0.3419, -0.9397] = -axis. Hmm, that means socket z points toward the head (into the head), i.e., the open face looks toward the head. Wait: if the socket face is at 50mm out on the axis (beyond the head top along the axis direction), and the socket is to engage the head, the socket must move in the -axis direction to reach the head. The socket's open face faces the head, so socket z (pointing out of open face) points toward the head, i.e., -axis.

Hmm, but earlier I reasoned socket z points out of socket. If the socket is beyond the head (farther along axis) and facing back toward the head, then its open face points in -axis direction, so socket z = -axis. Then as the socket moves along -axis (push negative? or push along socket z?), the socket goes onto the head.

Wait, "Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z." So if socket z points toward the head (into the head direction), pressing onto the head means moving in -socket z direction? Hmm.

Let's reconsider: tool z points out of the socket (from the flange, through the socket, out the open face). Actually the spec: "Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket." So tool z points out of the open face — away from the wrist, out the front of the socket.

When the socket is on the bolt, the open face is at the head (or beyond?), and z points out of the socket away from the wrist. The wrist is behind the socket. So if the socket is approaching the head from outside (in front of the module), the wrist is behind (farther out), and the socket open face touches the head. Tool z points from wrist through socket out the open face — toward the head and beyond. So tool z points along the bolt axis (out of head). Hmm, but then to seat, we move the socket in the -z direction (toward the head)? No wait.

Let me set coordinates: bolt head top at H. Axis a = (0, 0.342, 0.940) points out of head (away from module). The bolt shaft goes into the module along -a. The socket must go over the head from the outside, approaching along -a direction (from outside toward the head). The socket's open face faces the head, i.e., faces along -a. Tool z points out of the open face, so tool z points toward the head, i.e., -a = (0, -0.342, -0.940). Yes! That matches the ready aims' socket_toward = [0, -0.3419, -0.9397] ≈ -a.

And "50 mm out on the axis" position = H + 0.05*a = (0.420, 0.0321, 0.48599). That's the socket face 50mm beyond the head top along the axis (outside). The socket faces the head (z = -a). To seat, push in -z direction (i.e., along a? no...). Push moves "straight along the way the socket points" = along tool z = -a. Positive push moves along z = -a, i.e., toward the head. Good: push positive moves socket onto the head. And pressing onto surface reads negative force along tool z — when socket presses on head, the head pushes back on socket along +z (opposing motion into head), so force on tool is +z? They say negative force along tool z reads as pressing onto surface. Hmm, force that surroundings apply to tool: if socket pushes into head (motion along -a = z direction), head pushes back along +a = -z. So force on tool is along -z = negative z. Yes consistent: pressing → negative Fz.

OK so the plan:
1. Aim at 50 mm out: aim([0.420, 0.0321, 0.486], [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]).
2. seat: closed loop, starts with socket on axis just off head top, reached in two aims: first 50mm out aim, then centre 0.5mm out aim. seat handles centering, pressing lightly, turning slowly until hex flats line up and socket drops on. Ends when seated or max_s.
3. tighten_to(torque_Nm ~16): turn seated socket tightening direction (positive turn about tool z tightens right-hand thread). Stop at drive torque 16 Nm.
4. unload: turn back until drive torque near zero.
5. retract(mm=50): move socket straight out along axis until face 50mm from head top.
6. done.

But wait — there are conditions and limits. Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from zero. Bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug. So we need to turn up to 212 degrees to reach snug, then further to reach 14 Nm. Wrist 3 has limited range: "at most one full turn either way from its zero". Current wrist 3 joint position is -0.0412 rad. So range is [-1.0412, 0.9588] rad roughly (one full turn = 2π either way from zero: [-2π, 2π] from zero? "at most one full turn either way from its zero" — meaning wrist3 angle must stay within [-2π, 2π]? Or from its zero position? Current is -0.0412, near zero. So we have about ±2π ≈ 6.28 rad ≈ 360 degrees of travel. The bolt needs up to 212° to snug plus tightening to 14 Nm — could be more than 360° total? Possibly. "A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again." So we may need multiple seat-tighten-unload-retract-re-seat cycles? Hmm, but installed torque is cumulative — once snug, torque rises as turned further. If we have to lift and re-seat, we lose position? Actually unloading turns back until torque near zero, bolt stays tight. Then retract, then re-seat and tighten more. The installed torque is remembered by the bolt (it stays tight). So we can do multiple tightening bites.

But 30 seconds total! That's tight. Let's estimate: aim moves, seat (up to 10s), tighten (up to 15s), unload, retract. Total could exceed 30s. We need to be efficient.

Also time: "You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed." So we need to complete within 30 seconds of... tick 0 presumably. Each command takes time. We need to move fast but within limits.

Let's think about the sequence and timing:

Tick 0: current state. First command: aim to 50mm out. The arm moves from current pose to that aim. How long? The arm moves within limits; time depends on distance and speed limits. The readings say the aim moves the tool in a straight line. Duration isn't specified; result tells how it ended.

Then seat: needs two aims first per spec: "Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim." So we call aim (50mm out), then aim (0.5mm out), then seat. Actually seat itself does the closed loop starting from there. But we need to reach those positions via aim commands first.

Sequence:
1. aim(50mm out) — move there.
2. aim(0.5mm out) — move closer, centred.
3. seat(max_s=?) — engages socket.
4. tighten_to(16) — tighten to 16 Nm.
5. unload.
6. retract(50).
7. done.

Timing: Each aim move takes some seconds. Distance from current tool pos (0.2505, 0.1837, 0.5125) to 50mm out point (0.420, 0.0321, 0.486): delta = (0.1695, -0.1516, -0.0265), distance ≈ 0.228 m. Plus reorientation 22.5 deg tilt + yaw change. Arm speed limits: joints up to 2.094 rad/s for shoulder. Move time maybe ~1-2 s. Then aim 2: short move (0.5 mm + recentre) quick. Seat: up to 10s but likely faster. Tighten: bolt 149-212° short of snug; need to turn to snug then to 14 Nm. Tighten_to turns slowly, max 15s. Then unload (quick), retract (50mm out, quick).

Total might be ~10-20s. Should fit in 30s if each is efficient. But we don't know exact durations. We just proceed step by step, checking results.

Also torque limit: must not exceed 18 Nm installed. Aim for 16 (middle of 14-18). tighten_to stops when drive torque reaches torque_Nm; installed torque within ~0.1 of stop. Set 16.0 or 16.5. "aim for the middle (about 15.5-16)". Let's use 16.0.

But careful: tighten_to stops "as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm". Drive torque vs installed torque — approximately equal while tightening (socket grips). Fine.

Also the bolt starts between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug. We don't know exactly. tighten_to will turn until torque 16 Nm; passing through snug. Fine.

Wrist 3 range: current -0.0412 rad. Turning ~212° + more = up to maybe 300-400° total = 5-7 rad. One full turn either way from zero = 2π = 6.28 rad. Might be cutting close if bolt needs 212° to snug plus significant tightening. 14 Nm on an M8 — snug to 14 Nm might be 90-180 degrees? Total could be 212+180 = 392° = 6.84 rad > 6.28. Might exceed wrist range. Then we need to unload, retract, re-seat, tighten again. But 30s limit makes this risky. Let's first try and see results. The sensor feedback will tell.

Actually, "wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero" — zero of wrist 3, not current position. Current wrist3 is -0.0412, close to zero. So allowable range approximately [-6.28, 6.28] rad, and we start at -0.0412. Tightening uses positive turn (clockwise as seen from behind tool = positive). Positive direction: how much can we turn positive? Up to 6.28 - (-0.0412)? If limit is absolute wrist3 position within [-2π, 2π], then we can turn +6.32 rad ≈ 362 degrees. That's enough for 212° to snug + ~150° tightening. Might be OK.

But also during seat, "turn slowly until hex flats line up" — seat may turn the socket some degrees to align flats (hex repeats every 60°; up to 30° maybe). That uses wrist3 range too. Hmm.

Anyway, proceed and observe.

First command: aim to 50mm out.

messages.reasoning_content:
Interesting. Seat finished: "not seated after 10.0 s (turned 143 degrees)". But the readings show socket depth on the head: 2.03 mm (head top 2.03 mm inside socket), axis off 0.19 mm, tilt 0.49 deg. So actually it IS seated — depth 2.03 mm ≥ 2.5 mm? No, 2.03 < 2.5. Condition: "the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket". So depth 2.03 mm is not quite enough for the seated condition. But the seat command says not seated. Hmm, but the socket appears engaged (depth 2.03 mm, on axis, aligned). The seat command turned 143 degrees (trying to align flats) and didn't confirm "seated" — maybe it requires the socket to drop further onto the head. Depth is 2.03 mm inside; the socket face is 0.16 m from flange... depth of engagement maybe needs to be deeper.

Wait — seat turned 143 degrees. Wrist 3 went from -0.1961 to 2.2717 rad. That's +2.4678 rad = 141.4 degrees. Yes. So seat spun the socket trying to find the flat alignment. It ended not seated per its own criterion, but physically the socket is on the head (2.03 mm deep, centred, aligned).

Hmm, but "not seated" means the closed loop didn't achieve engagement. But readings show depth 2.03 mm. Maybe the socket is on the head but not fully down (the head needs to be at least 2.5 mm inside). Or maybe the socket is jammed askew? Tilt is 0.49 deg, off-axis 0.19 mm — looks fine. The depth 2.03 mm is close to 2.5 but short.

Options: The socket appears engaged enough to tighten? The tighten_to requires the socket seated. Condition for job: depth ≥ 2.5 mm. Currently 2.03 mm. If I tighten now, turning the socket would drive it deeper? Actually tightening turns the socket about its axis; the socket is already on the head. If the socket is engaged (hex flats aligned), turning tightens the bolt. The depth might increase as the bolt is drawn in? No — the bolt head is fixed in the clamp; turning the socket rotates the bolt, driving it into the threaded hole. The socket depth on the head stays the same (socket sits on head top).

So depth 2.03 mm < 2.5 mm fails the seated condition. Hmm. But maybe seat didn't fully complete because it hit its internal criteria. The socket might be sitting on the head but the flats aren't fully engaged (it turned 143° looking for alignment; hex repeats every 60°, so it tried multiple positions).

Actually wait: socket depth 2.03 mm — the head top is 2.03 mm inside the socket. The socket is 13mm hex; the head presumably fits. If the socket is slightly cocked or the hex corners are catching, depth is limited. Seat says not seated.

Can I call seat again? The spec says seat starts with socket on axis just off head top, reached in two aims. Currently socket is at depth 2.03 mm (already on the head). Re-running seat from here might not follow the protocol. Alternatively, maybe I should just try tighten_to — if the socket is engaged (gripping flats), tightening will work, and depth might not matter for the tool. But the job condition requires ≥ 2.5 mm depth.

Hmm, let me reconsider: maybe the seat turned 143 degrees and the socket is now engaged but the depth reading of 2.03 mm is what it is. Perhaps the socket face is at the head top plus the socket's internal depth — the "depth on the head" might be how far the head protrudes into the socket. function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.

- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.
