function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. function.name: push

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.

- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.

- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.

- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.

- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. # Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. # Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.

- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: unload

# Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands

function.name: aim

function.name: push

function.name: turn

function.name: push_and_turn

- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.

- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.

You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. # Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. # Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.

- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.

## Readings worked out for you
Each round also gives, computed from the head position and axis the work order states (to the millimetre it is printed in) and the tool pose: where the top of the head is, how deep the socket is on it (said in words), how far and which way the socket is off the bolt's axis, the angle between them, and three ready commands: one that centres the socket on the axis where it is now, one that centres it 0.5 mm out from the head top, and one that puts it 50 mm out on the axis. They are only as exact as the work order's numbers, about half a millimetre.

# Work order: tighten a module clamp bolt

Tighten the clamp bolt in front of the robot into the module manufacturer's torque window, then take the tool away.

The bolt is an M8 with a hex head and a right-hand thread. The centre of the top of its head is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439) m in the base frame, and its axis points out of the head along (-0.000, 0.342, 0.940). The bolt starts loose, between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug, with its flats at any angle. Installed torque is the tightening torque the bolt has reached; it is near zero until the bolt is snug and rises as the bolt is turned further.

The job is judged on the conditions below, in this order, and on nothing else.
- The socket is seated on the head: the top of the head at least 2.5 mm inside the socket, with the socket's axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees of the bolt's.
- The bolt has been turned until it is snug, the point where the clamp starts to resist.
- The installed torque has reached 14 N·m.
- The socket is off the head, its face more than 30 mm from the top of the head.
- If the installed torque goes above 18 N·m at any moment, the clamp is damaged and the job has failed, whatever happens afterwards.

You have 30 s. A job that is not finished by then has failed.

Let me analyze the current state and plan the task.

The goal: tighten a clamp bolt to 14-18 N·m (aim ~15.5-16), then retract the tool off the head (>30 mm from head top). Conditions:
1. Socket seated on head (head top at least 2.5 mm inside socket, axis within 1.2 mm and 6 degrees).
2. Bolt turned until snug.
3. Installed torque reaches 14 N·m (don't exceed 18).
4. Socket off head, face >30 mm from head top.
5. Never exceed 18 N·m.

The bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). Tool z should point along the bolt axis for the socket to engage. The ready aims have socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397] — wait, that's the negative of the bolt axis? The bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). The socket's z points out of the socket. To seat the socket onto the bolt head, the socket's axis should point toward the head... Hmm, let's think.

The socket face is 0.16 m from the wrist flange along the wrist-3 axis (tool z). The socket's open face is at the tool origin? Actually "Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket." So tool z points out of the socket (away from the head when seated). The bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). So when seated, tool z should align with the bolt axis (both pointing out of the head). So socket_toward should be [0, 0.342, 0.940]? But the ready aims say [0, -0.3419, -0.9397] — that's the opposite direction!

Wait, let's reconsider. The ready aim "to put it 50 mm out from the head top on the axis": aim [0.420, 0.03210, 0.48599]. Head top is at (0.420, 0.015, 0.439). The difference: (0, 0.0171, 0.04699). The bolt axis direction is (0, 0.342, 0.940). 50 mm along the axis: 0.05*(0, 0.342, 0.940) = (0, 0.0171, 0.047). So aim = head top + 50mm along bolt axis. So the "50 mm out" point is in the direction the bolt axis points (out of the head). The socket_toward for that aim is [0, -0.3419, -0.9397], i.e., pointing back toward the head. So the socket z points toward the head (into the socket? no...).

Hmm, tool z points out of the socket. If the socket is 50 mm out from the head top along the bolt axis, and socket z points back toward the head (-bolt axis direction), then the socket face points toward the head. To seat, you move the socket forward (push) along its z... wait push moves along the socket's pointing direction. If socket z points toward the head, pushing moves the socket toward the head, engaging it. But tool z points "out of the socket" — meaning out of the open face? If the open face faces the head, then z pointing out of the socket would point toward the head. Yes! The socket's open face is where the head goes; z points out of the socket through the open face, i.e., toward the head when approaching. So socket z = -bolt axis direction = (0, -0.342, -0.940) when approaching from in front of the head.

Wait, but the bolt axis points out of the head along (0, 0.342, 0.940). "Out of the head" — the head sits on a surface, the axis points outward from the head (away from the clamped parts). The socket approaches the head from the outside, so the socket is located further along the bolt axis beyond the head top. The socket z points toward the head, i.e., opposite to the bolt axis: (0, -0.342, -0.940). Yes, that matches the ready aims.

When seated, the socket's axis aligns with the bolt axis but the socket z still points toward the head (into the clamped assembly), while the bolt axis points out of the head. So they're anti-parallel? The condition says "socket's axis within ... 6 degrees of the bolt's" — axis as a line, direction probably ignored (or they consider the line). Fine.

So the plan:
1. Aim at "50 mm out" point: aim [0.420, 0.03210, 0.48599], socket_toward [0, -0.3419, -0.9397]. This is the safe approach.
2. Then aim at "centre it 0.5 mm out from head top": [0.420, 0.01517, 0.43947], same direction.
3. Then seat (closed loop): it says start with socket on axis just off head top, reached in two aims: first 50 mm out, then centre 0.5 mm out. Then seat() engages the socket onto the head.
4. tighten_to(15.5-16) to reach installed torque ~15.5-16 N·m (accepts 14-18, aim middle).
5. unload() to release grip.
6. retract(mm=50) to move socket face 50 mm from head top (>30 mm clears condition).

Also need to consider wrist 3 rotation limit: at most one full turn either way from zero. The bolt starts between 149 and 212 degrees short of snug. Hmm, "short of snug" means it needs tightening by 149-212 degrees to reach snug? Then more to reach 14 N·m. Total rotation might be more than 360? Let's think: 149-212 degrees to snug, then additional rotation to reach torque. Could exceed one full turn (360 degrees)? Wrist 3 can turn at most one full turn either way from zero. If needed more, lift socket, turn back, seat again. Hmm, but seat() handles unwinding if a corner catches.

Actually the turn() command is limited to 90 degrees at a time. tighten_to is closed loop and handles turning until torque reached, presumably handling multiple turns? It says "turn the seated socket in the tightening direction... stop as soon as drive torque reaches torque_Nm". Probably can rotate multiple turns internally. The wrist 3 limit: "Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again." So if the required rotation exceeds remaining wrist-3 range, we'd need to unload, retract, rotate wrist 3 back toward zero, re-seat, and continue. But tighten_to presumably manages this internally? Not necessarily. Let's first check current wrist 3 position: 0.0073 rad ≈ 0.4 degrees. So nearly full range available (±1 turn = ±2π ≈ 6.28 rad). The bolt needs 149-212 degrees to snug plus more to torque. Could be up to ~212 + some degrees. Possibly under 360. Let's proceed and see.

Time limit: 30 seconds. We need to be efficient.

Let me plan the sequence:

Tick 0: Call aim to 50mm out point.
Then aim to 0.5mm out.
Then seat(max_s=...).
Then tighten_to(15.5 or 16).
Then unload.
Then retract(50).
Then done.

But careful: the aim commands move the arm; each takes time. We have 30s total. Movements should be fast enough. Let's just go step by step, observing results.

First call: aim to the 50 mm out point.

aim = [0.42000, 0.03210, 0.48599], socket_toward = [0.0000, -0.3419, -0.9397].

Let me start.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

message.reasoning_content: Socket face is 0.33 mm short of head top, centred (0.10 mm off, 0.09° tilt). Now call seat() to engage the socket onto the head.

function.name: aim
function.description: Put the centre of the socket's open face at a point, with the open face pointing along a direction, both in the base frame. The tool turns as little as it can to get there, in a straight line: from far away, stop 50 mm out on the bolt's axis first (the readings' ready aim) before closing in on the head.

aim.description: the point [x, y, z] in metres

socket_toward.description: the direction tool z points; need not be a unit vector

function.name: push
function.description: Move the tool straight along the way the socket points, keeping its orientation. Negative moves it back.

function.name: turn
function.description: Turn the tool about its own z axis, keeping its position. Positive turns clockwise as seen from behind the tool, which tightens a right-hand thread. At most 90 degrees; more is cut to 90.

function.name: push_and_turn
function.description: Both at once: turn while pressing (or pulling) along the socket's axis.

function.name: pose
function.description: Send the tool frame to a pose in the base frame.

function.name: done
function.description: The job is finished or cannot be finished.

function.name: seat
function.description: Closed loop: keep the socket centred on the bolt's axis, press lightly and turn slowly until the hex flats line up and the socket drops onto the head (engaged), unwinding if a corner catches. Start with the socket on the axis just off the head top, reached in two aims: first the readings' ready 'put it 50 mm out' aim, then the ready 'centre it 0.5 mm out from the head top' aim. A single move straight from far away can clip the head and jam the socket on it askew, and seat cannot recover from that. Ends when seated, or after max_s seconds.

function.name: tighten_to
function.description: Closed loop: turn the seated socket in the tightening direction, keeping it pressed on and centred, slowing near the end, and stop as soon as the wrist's drive torque reaches torque_Nm. The installed torque ends within about 0.1 N·m of where it stops. The job accepts 14 to 18 N·m installed, so aim for the middle (about 15.5-16) to keep a margin on both sides. Ends then, or if the socket comes off, or after max_s seconds.

torque_Nm.description: drive torque to stop at, in N·m

function.name: unload
function.description: Closed loop: turn back slowly, keeping the socket on, until the drive torque is near zero (under 0.1 N·m), so the socket no longer grips the flats. The bolt stays tight. Do this before retract: a socket still loaded grips the flats and the retract sticks.

function.name: retract
function.description: Closed loop: move the socket straight out along the bolt's axis until its face is mm millimetres from the head top, keeping it centred and straight. Unload first. 50 mm or more clears the job's 30 mm condition with a margin.

mm.description: distance of the socket face from the head top, mm

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.

- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. # Your body: a Universal Robots UR16e arm on a parked Clearpath Husky A300

You control a six-joint industrial arm. It is bolted to a wheeled base that is parked and does not move. A socket for 13 mm hex heads is fixed rigidly to the last joint, wrist 3. There is no powered tool: the wrist itself turns the socket.

## Frames and units
- Everything is in SI units: metres, radians, seconds, newtons, newton-metres.
- Base frame: origin at the base of the arm, x forward, y left, z up.
- Tool frame: origin at the centre of the socket's open face, z along the socket's axis, pointing out of the socket.
- An orientation is a unit quaternion in the order x, y, z, w.
- A positive rotation about tool z turns a fastener clockwise as seen from behind the tool. That tightens a right-hand thread.

## Tool
- The socket's face is 0.16 m from the wrist-3 flange, on the wrist-3 axis.
- The socket is a hex 13.3 mm across flats. It only goes over a head whose flats line up with its own, and those repeat every 60 degrees.

## Limits
- Joint torque limits in N·m: shoulder pan 330, shoulder lift 330, elbow 150, wrist 1 54, wrist 2 54, wrist 3 54.
- Joint speed limits in rad/s: shoulder pan and lift 2.094, elbow 3.142, wrists 3.142.
- Wrist 3 turns at most one full turn either way from its zero. A job that needs more rotation than is left has to lift the socket, turn back and seat it again.
- A commanded pose that the arm cannot reach within these limits is not reached. Nothing is done for you.

## Senses
- Joint positions and velocities, and the pose of the tool frame in the base frame.
- A force-torque sensor at the wrist-3 flange gives the force (N) and torque (N·m) that the surroundings apply to the tool, in the tool frame. It reads zero while the tool touches nothing.
- Pressing the socket onto a surface reads as a negative force along tool z.
- While the socket tightens a bolt, the bolt's resistance reads as a negative torque about tool z, equal in size to the tightening torque.

## Commands
You act through the tools you are given: call exactly one tool each turn. The arm moves the tool within its limits and stops when it arrives, when it can go no further, or when the command's time runs out; the tool's result then tells you how the command ended and what the robot senses. Keep calling tools until the job is finished or cannot be finished, then call done.
